tracking.name: Global Fire Management Hub
tracking.description: To reduce wildfire emissions and strengthen climate resilience by advancing integrated fire management that combines science and Indigenous knowledge to promote sustainable fire use and lower destructive wildfire intensity globally.
tracking.indicator: Reduction of destructive wildfire risk and emissions through integrated fire management
tracking.findings: Fire Hub and PAS partners supported integrated fire management approaches in more than 30 countries during the reporting period. Progress included capacity development, strengthened regional networks, improved knowledge and data sharing, fire risk reduction and early warning, community and Indigenous-led approaches, and support to IFM policy and governance.

cases.title: Scaling implementation and capacity for integrated fire management (IFM)
cases.initiative: by the Global Fire Management Hub
cases.target: Related CCI target: Reduction of destructive wildfire risk and emissions through integrated fire management
cases.contribution: This action is reported as contributing to Objective 6. Efforts to conserve, protect and restore nature and ecosystems with solutions for climate, biodiversity and desertification.
body: During September 2025–August 2026, the Global Fire Management Hub (Fire Hub) and partners supported implementation of integrated fire management (IFM) in more than 30 countries. Through the Plan to Accelerate Solutions (PAS), Fire Hub projects and related partner initiatives, governments, international and regional organizations, civil society and other partners worked to strengthen national and regional capacities to prevent, prepare for and manage wildfire risk.

Implementation covered multiple dimensions of IFM, including capacity development and training, fire risk reduction and early warning, improved access to fire knowledge and data, policy and governance support, and community-based and Indigenous-led approaches to fire management. Activities sought to support the transition from predominantly reactive fire suppression towards proactive, risk-informed approaches that place greater emphasis on prevention, preparedness and resilience while recognizing the appropriate use of beneficial fire. The action directly supports the Fire Hub's overarching NAZCA target of supporting partners in 30 countries to implement IFM approaches that reduce the rate and intensity of destructive wildfires, lower associated greenhouse-gas emissions and strengthen resilience.

The “Basic integrated fire management tools for early warning and decision-making” online course, launched in April 2026, had been accessed by more than 1,000 learners by September. In addition, the working groups (with PAS partners as participants) have produced concrete tools to support fire practitioners and land managers. The Fire Hub Working Group on Data, for example, has produced a catalogue of national, regional and global data sets and identified how each contributes to pre-fire risk mitigation, early warning and preparation, during fire operational response, and post-fire recovery and rehabilitation.

Together, these results demonstrate progress across the five strategic pillars of the Global Fire Management Hub: knowledge and data sharing; capacity building; wildfire-resilient communities; fire risk reduction and early warning; and IFM policy development and implementation.

cases.title: High-level signing of the Climate-Resilient Coral Reefs Commitment at five multilateral convenings
cases.initiative: by the Global Commitment to Protect Climate-Resilient Coral Reefs
cases.target: Related CCI targets: 80 per cent of global coral reefs under political commitment; 31 signatory governments by COP 31; 50 global organizations support the climate-resilient coral reefs commitment by end of 2026
body: The Commitment has organized or co-organized high-level events at five major multilateral convenings since its launch (Third UN Ocean Conference, COP 30, UNEA-7, 11th Our Ocean Conference, and 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting), each designed to provide a formal moment for governments to accede and to raise the political visibility of climate-resilient coral reef protection.

Ahead of and during each event, new supporting organizations were welcomed to the Coral Commitment. Each event was designed to match the key priorities of each conference and to include interventions from signatories highlighting initiatives they are leading to implement the Commitment. The goal was also, each time, to rally all the actors working towards coral reef restoration.

Structured signing moments at multilateral convenings have proven the most effective mechanism for government accession. They give ministers and heads of delegation a defined, low-burden opportunity to join, with visibility and peer recognition attached. The events also bring signatory governments, scientific institutions, financing mechanisms, frontline community representatives and implementing organizations into the same room, enabling the practical conversations about implementation that follow signature.

These five convenings have delivered the majority of the Commitment's accessions to date, growing the coalition from eleven signatories at launch to 23, and rallying a total of 45 global organizations.

The UNEA-7 event coincided with the adoption of UNEA Resolution 1 on accelerating global action to promote the climate resilience of coral reefs, linking the Commitment's non-state ambition to a Member State mandate.
